description_full: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited, together with its subsidiaries, manufactures, packages, tests, and sells integrated circuits and other semiconductor devices in Taiwan, China, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Japan, the United States, and internationally. It provides various wafer fabrication processes, such as processes to manufacture complementary metal- oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) logic, mixed-signal, radio frequency, embedded memory, bipolar CMOS mixed-signal, and others. The company also involved in providing customer and engineering support services; manufacturing of masks; investment in technology start-up companies; research, designing, developing, manufacturing, packaging, testing, and sale of color filters; and investment activities. Its products are used in high performance computing, smartphones, Internet of things, automotive, and digital consumer electronics. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited was incorporated in 1987 and is headquartered in Hsinchu City, Taiwan.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 76K people. Revenue per employee of $1.2M ranks in the top quartile among Technology peers, with revenue growing 16%/yr across its filed history. financial_summary: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufactur is a mega-cap technology business with a $2.1T market cap on $90.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +17% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 48% against a 11% cost of capital — a 37-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 52% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $27.1B in free cash flow — roughly 30 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.58× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.6%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
